verdicts.trueWording: It detaches the tale from a narrow context
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of brightweavings.com/globe/ (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200). Quote exact in the 'what can fantasy do better' paragraph: 'First of all the genre allows the universalizing of a story... It detaches the tale from a narrow context, permits a stripping away, or at least an eroding of prejudices and assumptions.' The subject of 'It' is the fantasy genre, so the claim's limb about setting a story as fantasy holds.

verdicts.trueWording: Fantasy, in this light, becomes a way of being honest about limitations
verdicts.note: Raw page. Exact sentence in the Henry James paragraph, preceded by 'by treating the past through the form of a fantasy, one acknowledges the sort of difficulties James was referring to' — both limbs (treating the past as fantasy; honesty about limitations) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Douglas Barbour described a fantasy he admired as that escape
verdicts.note: Raw page, closing paragraph: 'Many years ago, the poet and critic, Douglas Barbour, described a fantasy he admired as, ‘The kind of escape that brings you home.’ I realized, reading these words, that this was how I’d always seen the potential of the genre.' Attribution to Barbour and Kay's endorsement both explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: All renderings matter; in the changes we find truths about evolving worlds and societies
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of brightweavings.com/mythessay/ (HTTP 200). First body paragraph: 'All renderings matter, and in the changes, the shiftings, we find truths about evolving worlds and societies.' Page header confirms the source: written summer 1999 for the Chapters 'Great Writers' series, run as full-page newspaper inserts. Kay's wording is 'evolving worlds and societies' rather than the claim's 'societies that made them'; in context (renderings shifting as generations and cultures change) the limb is supported, but the claim's phrasing is a gloss, not Kay's.

verdicts.trueWording: the earliest version of a legend isn’t always the most important
verdicts.note: Raw page, first body paragraph: 'One of the first things learned in the study of myth is that the earliest version of a legend isn’t always the the most important.' (The doubled 'the the' is a typo on the page; the quoted fragment matches character-for-character.)

verdicts.trueWording: I tried to imagine myself with a stiletto not a bludgeon
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of brightweavings.com/tiganaafterword/ (HTTP 200); header confirms the ROC USA 10th anniversary edition of Tigana, 1999. Penultimate paragraph: 'I tried to imagine myself with a stiletto not a bludgeon, slipping the themes of the story in quietly while keeping a reader turning pages well past bedtime.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: I wanted to start a book about subterfuge and deception with an outright lie
verdicts.note: Raw page: 'I wanted to start a book about subterfuge and deception with an outright lie – and the first sentence of chapter one does that. I wanted to work with music...' — confirms both the intent limb and the first-sentence-of-chapter-one limb, and the located paragraph does go on to music.

verdicts.trueWording: registered powerfully for me, and lingered for twenty years: not only killed, but made to never have been
verdicts.note: Raw page, photograph paragraph: two LIFE-magazine Prague Spring photographs, the second missing one functionary with a plant inserted; 'The missing figure – part of the crushed uprising – is not only dead, he has been erased from the record... the two photographs registered powerfully for me, and lingered for twenty years: not only killed, but made to never have been.' The seeding limb is supported by the framing 'a reconstruction of the earliest seeds of the book'.

verdicts.trueWording: Names link to history, and we need a sense of our history to define ourselves
verdicts.note: Raw page, Brian Friel 'Translations' paragraph; the sentence carries both limbs of the claim verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: fantasy has never been in its essence about... variations on the use of hyphens and apostrophes in invented names
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of brightweavings.com/earthlight/ (HTTP 200); header confirms it was written for Earthlight, GGK's British publishing house. The rejection limb is explicit: 'For me, fantasy has never been in its essence about constructing elaborate magical systems... or further variations on the use of hyphens and apostrophes in invented names.'

verdicts.trueWording: I am happy establishing a space between the invented character and the real man
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of brightweavings.com/underheavenauthorsletter/ (HTTP 200); header confirms it was first printed in the advance reading copies of Under Heaven, 2010. The sentence closes the paragraph about the real Tang prime minister versus 'my prime minister of Ninth Dynasty Kitai'.

verdicts.trueWording: I’ve served notice with the shift to an imagined Kitai from real China that I reserve the right to change, or telescope events
verdicts.note: Raw page. The sentence sits in the paragraph opening 'I want to keep readers turning pages until two in the morning', exactly as the claim's page hint says; both limbs (the shift serves notice; the reserved right to change or telescope) are explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: the quiet, steady accumulation of detail and complexity reach out to readers in an almost subliminal way
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of brightweavings.com/sfsite/ (HTTP 200); header confirms an interview conducted by Rodger Turner, September 2000, reproduced from SFSite. In the answer that opens 'Depends what one means by the ‘credibility of the book’', followed by 'Readers end up with a measure of trust in the author and the book... and that trust is invaluable' — the trust limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: what we know of the great figures of the past is so much shaped by (at the mercy of!) those who chronicled them
verdicts.note: Raw page, the answer on legacy and posterity: '...and Procopius’s malevolent The Secret History is a perfect example of that, vis a vis Justinian and Theodora.' Both the shaped-by/at-the-mercy-of limb and the Procopius citation limb are explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: A viewpoint character observing a setting for the first time serves wonderfully as a ‘window’ for the reader
verdicts.note: Raw page, the 'fish out of water' answer: the quoted sentence is followed by 'The initiation of a character becomes the reader’s initiation.', supporting the claim's second limb.
